title: 7-Point Set Tiebreak
text: 7-Point Set Tiebreak. The 7-Point Set Tiebreak is played when the players reach 6-all in a set. The first player or team to win 7 points by a margin of at least 2 wins the set 7-6.

title: 10-Point Match Tiebreak
text: 10-Point Match Tiebreak. The 10-Point Match Tiebreak is played in some matches in lieu of the deciding final set. The first player or team to win 10 points by a margin of at least 2 wins the final set 1-0 and the match.

title: Abandoned Match
text: Abandoned Match. An Abandoned Match refers to a match that was started, but the Referee has decided not to complete the match.

title: Adult Age Group Divisions
text: Adult Age Group Divisions. As a group, the Adult Divisions with age restrictions are known as the Adult Age Group Divisions. This does not include any Adult NTRP Division that has an age restriction.

title: Adult Discipline
text: Adult Discipline. Adult Discipline occurs when a parent, coach, or other adult responsible for a Junior disciplines the Junior by not allowing the Junior to start or finish a match. Adult Discipline is treated as a Default if the match has not started and as a Retirement if the match has started. Adult Discipline is never recorded as a Withdrawal or Walkover.

title: Adult Divisions
text: Adult Divisions. These divisions comprise the Open Men’s, Women’s, and Mixed Doubles; Men’s, Women’s and Mixed Age divisions beginning at 25 and older Divisions; and NTRP and other level-based Divisions based on ratings.

title: Advantage (Ad) Court
text: Advantage (Ad) Court: The advantage court refers to the service court that is on a player’s side of the net to the left of the center service line as a player faces the net. The court is called the advantage or ad court because points in which the score is “Advantage” are always served to this court.

title: Advantage Scoring
text: Advantage Scoring. This is the traditional scoring system in which the points are 15, 30, 40, Deuce, and Advantage.

title: Advantage Set
text: Advantage Set. This is a set in which a Set Tiebreak is not played when the score reaches 6-6 and continues until one player leads the opponent by a margin of two games. Advantage sets are no longer played under USTA Regulations. Occasionally an advantage set ends up being played when the players forget to play a Set Tiebreak at 6-6.

title: All-Factors Method of Seeding
text: All-Factors Method of Seeding. This seeding method is based on the players’ chances of winning the tournament as determined by the Tournament Committee.

title: Alley
text: Alley. The alley is the area between the singles sideline and the doubles sideline.

title: Alphabetical Seeding
text: Alphabetical Seeding. In some cases the Tournament Committee may group seeded players together and assign each of them the same seed (for example, in the group 5-8, each player in the group is assigned the fifth seed and listed alphabetically).

title: Alternate
text: Alternate. An alternate is a player who did not make it into the draw but requests that the tournament consider the player for entry into the draw if an opening in the draw develops.

title: Alternate List
text: Alternate List. The alternate list is a list of players not accepted into a tournament. After entries close, the Tournament Committee will typically publish an ordered alternate list showing the order in which the alternates will be accepted if there is a withdrawal.

title: Amateur
text: Amateur. A player is an amateur if the player does not receive and has not received, directly or indirectly, pecuniary advantage by the playing, teaching, demonstrating, or pursuit of the game of tennis except as specifically authorized by USTA Regulation XIX.

title: Back Draw
text: Back Draw. This term is commonly used to describe any consolation draw.

title: Baselines
text: Baselines. The baselines are the lines at the ends of the court.

title: Bleeding Timeout
text: Bleeding Timeout. A Bleeding Timeout is a time-out of up to 15 minutes that is allowed when a player is bleeding externally. The time is used to stop the bleeding and to clean up the playing area.

title: Blended Lines
text: Blended Lines. Blended Lines has a narrow definition and a broad definition. The lines on the regulation 78-foot court are painted white. Sometimes permanent lines for Red Ball Tennis and Orange Ball Tennis are also painted on the court. These lines should be painted a lighter or darker shade of the color of the court surface. The narrower definition of blended lines refers to these lines only. Courts with blended lines as defined in the narrow sense may be used for almost all matches except certain ITF events. The broader definition of blended lines refers to courts with lines used by sports other than tennis such as pickle ball, badminton, or basketball. Absent the applicable sanctioning body prohibiting matches on courts with blended lines in the broader sense, the Referee determines whether matches may be played on these courts.

title: Block Seeding
text: Block Seeding. Block seeding refers to the practice of taking the seeded players and advancing them two or more rounds into the tournament. The unseeded players play matches to reach the round where the seeded players have already been stationed. The purpose of this practice is to allow all the unseeded players to play several matches before facing a seeded player.

title: Bonus Points
text: Bonus Points. Bonus points are additional ranking points that are awarded for wins over highly ranked players.

title: Bye
text: Bye. When there are not enough players or teams to put on each line, byes are placed on the open lines. A player or team who receives a bye does not have a first round match.

title: Cancelled Match
text: Cancelled Match. A cancelled match refers to a match that the Referee decides will not be played for any reason other than a disqualification, withdrawal, walkover, or default.

title: Center Marks
text: Center Marks. The center marks are the 2-inch wide marks that are placed just inside each baseline and that mark the precise middle of the baselines. The center marks line up with the center service line.

title: Center Service Line
text: Center Service Line. The center service line is the line that divides the service lines and the service courts in half. The line is 2 inches wide and 42 feet long.

title: Chair Umpire
text: Chair Umpire. The Chair Umpire is the official responsible for conducting one match in accordance with the ITF Rules of Tennis and the USTA Regulations.

title: Changeover
text: Changeover. The changeover is the 90-second period after the end of every odd game (other than the first game) of every set.

title: Chief Umpire
text: Chief Umpire. A Chief Umpire is an official responsible for hiring the officials. In many tournaments, the Referee will delegate to the Chief Umpire the responsibility for assigning, replacing, and reassigning officials.

title: Circuit
text: Circuit. A series of tournaments that are organized as a group and generally adopt a common set of special tournament regulations.

title: Closed Tournament
text: Closed Tournament. A closed tournament is a tournament that is limited to residents of a particular geographic area.

title: The Code
text: The Code. The Code is a summary of the procedures and unwritten rules that custom dictates that players follow. USTA Regulation IV.B. requires players to follow The Code in all matches without officials.

title: Code Violation
text: Code Violation. Code violations are issued to players for misconduct and delay. A list of code violations and penalties is found in Table 14.

title: Coed Tournament
text: Coed Tournament. Players may enter a coed tournament regardless of gender. Any combination of males and females is permitted in singles and doubles.

title: Coman Tiebreak Procedure
text: Coman Tiebreak Procedure. The Coman Tiebreak Procedure requires the Tiebreak to be played with the players changing ends after the first point and thereafter every fourth point.

title: Combined Ranking
text: Combined Ranking. A combined ranking is a ranking that is based on both singles and doubles Ranking Points.

title: Compass Draw
text: Compass Draw. This is a non-elimination format that is so named because players advance in four to eight different directions depending upon when they lose their first match and when they lose their subsequent matches.

title: Computerized List Method of Seeding
text: Computerized List Method of Seeding. This seeding method is based on a computerized system of rankings, ratings, or standings.

title: Consolation Draw
text: Consolation Draw. A consolation draw describes a group of different types of draws in which losers in the main draw play an additional match or matches against other players who have lost a match in the main draw.

title: Court
text: Court. The term technically refers only to the area bounded by the baselines and the singles sidelines in singles and the doubles sidelines in doubles.

title: Curtis Consolation Draw of 64
text: Curtis Consolation Draw of 64. This type of Feed-In Championship is often used when there is a shortage of time or courts. A Curtis Consolation Draw of 64 feeds the Round of 64 and Round of 32 losers into one draw with the winner placing 13th. It also feeds the Round of 16 and Quarterfinal losers into another draw with the winner placing 5th.

title: Default
text: Default. A default occurs when a player is eliminated from an event under the Point Penalty System (which includes penalties for lateness) or refuses to play for reasons other than injury, illness, or personal circumstance. It is also considered a default when a junior does not start a match because of an adult deciding to discipline the junior. (Note that failure to finish a match because of an adult discipline is considered a retirement.)

title: Deputy Referee
text: Deputy Referee. A Deputy Referee is an official appointed by the Referee or Tournament Committee to assist in the performance of the Referee’s duties or to assume these duties when the Referee is absent. It is not unusual for a Deputy Referee to assist in making the draw or to serve as the Referee at a secondary site.

title: Deuce Court
text: Deuce Court. The deuce court refers to the service court that is on a player’s side of the net to the right of the center service line as a player faces the net. The court is called the deuce court because points in which the score is “Deuce” are always served to this court.

title: Disqualification
text: Disqualification. A disqualification occurs when a player is removed from an event because the player was ineligible for the event.

title: District Associations
text: District Associations. The term refers not only to traditional District Associations but also to other subdivisions of Sectional Associations.

title: Division
text: Division. Division refers to one or two events in a tournament in which the eligibility criteria are identical. For example, the Girls’ 16 Singles and Girls’ 16 Doubles are two events but only one division because their eligibility criteria are identical.

title: Doubles Sidelines
text: Doubles Sidelines. The doubles sidelines are the two lines that define the width of the court for doubles.

title: Electronic Line Calling (ELC)
text: Electronic Line Calling (ELC). “Electronic Line Calling” refers to electronic systems that determine whether a given ball impact is “in” or “out.” ELC systems can either be “Review” or “Live.” Review systems require the player to challenge the call of their opponent or an official. Live systems make audible and/or visual calls without requiring a player-initiated challenge. Systems that meet the minimum requirements for use in USTA sanctioned tournaments are published at usta.com. Only eligible ELC “Review” systems are authorized for use in USTA sanctioned play.

title: Entry Fee
text: Entry Fee. The entry fee is the fee paid for a player to enter a tournament. Players may also be charged a non-refundable fee that is not part of the entry fee for electronic entries.

title: Entry Level Tournament
text: Entry Level Tournament. This is the first or lowest level or levels of sanctioned play recognized by a Sectional or District Association. Entry Level Tournaments in the Junior divisions are part of the USTA Junior Circuit and are governed by the USTA Net Generation Pathway Regulations.

title: Event
text: Event. In the narrow sense, this term refers to one draw in a tournament. For example, the Girls’ 16 Singles and Girls’ 16 Doubles are two separate events within the same division—the Girls’ 16 division. The main draw, any associated consolation, and place-playoffs are considered one event. Sometimes this term is also used to refer to an entire tournament.

title: Family Divisions
text: Family Divisions. The Father-Son, Father (60 & Over)-Son, Father (70 & Over)-Son, Father-Daughter, Father (60 & Over)-Daughter, Father (70 & Over)- Daughter, Father (80 & Over)-Daughter, Mother-Son, Mother-Daughter, Mother (60 & Over)-Daughter, Mother (70 & Over)-Daughter, Husband-Wife Mixed, Husband- Wife Mixed (Combined Ages 100 years), Husband-Wife Mixed (Combined Ages 120 years), Husband-Wife Mixed (Combined Ages 140 years), and Grandfather- Grandson divisions comprise the Family divisions.

title: Feed-In Championship
text:
Feed-In Championship. This term, commonly abbreviated as FIC, refers to a consolation draw in which the losers from multiple rounds in the main draw are fed back into another draw or draws against players who lost in earlier rounds of the tournament. Most FICs have a playoff for 3rd and 4th place. There are several types of Feed-In Championships:
• An FIC that feeds in losers through the Quarterfinal with the winner of the consolation placing 5th.
• An FIC that feeds in losers through the Round of 16 with the winner of the FIC placing 9th and the Quarterfinal losers feed into a separate draw with the winner placing 5th.
• A Modified FIC that feeds in at least the first two rounds into the consolation, but fewer rounds that would classify the draw as one of the other FICs.
• A Curtis Consolation Draw of 64 that feeds the Round of 64 and Round of 32 losers into one draw with the winner placing 13th and also feeds the Round of 16 and Quarterfinal losers into another draw with the winner placing 5th.

title: First Match Consolation
text: First Match Consolation. This is a consolation draw in which the losers in the first round and those second round losers who advanced to that round by virtue of a bye or a default are entered into the consolation draw.

title: First Round Consolation
text: First Round Consolation. This is a consolation draw in which only the losers in the first round are entered into the consolation draw.

title: Flighting
text: Flighting. This is a method of distributing players entered in an event into separate draws so that players of the same level are in the same draw and compete against each other.

title: Garman System
text: Garman System. A staggered start time scheduling method based on statistical analysis of the length of matches. The system reduces player waiting time and maximizes court usage.

title: Green Ball Tennis
text: Green Ball Tennis. Green Ball Tennis is played on a 78-foot court with a stage 1 (green) ball.

title: Group Seeding
text: Group Seeding. In some cases the Tournament Committee may group seed players together and assign each of them the same seed (for example, in the group 5-8, each player in the group is assigned the fifth seed and is typically listed alphabetically).

title: Handshake
text: Handshake. By shaking hands the players have acknowledged the match is over. See Code 2.

title: Head-to-Head Ranking System
text: Head-to-Head Ranking System. This is a method of ranking players or teams that is based on wins, losses, and exposure.

title: Hindrance
text: Hindrance. A hindrance refers to a situation in which a player is hindered from making a shot by anything that is not within the player’s control other than a permanent fixture or a spectator’s outcry.

title: Inclement Weather
text: Inclement Weather. Inclement weather may cause a Referee to suspend or postpone matches, lengthen rest between matches, or shorten a tournament to keep it on schedule.

title: Incomplete Match
text: Incomplete Match. An incomplete match refers to a match that was started but not completed. It is anticipated that the match will be completed.

title: Intersectionals
text: Intersectionals. These are team tournaments in the Adult and Junior divisions in which teams compete against teams from other Sectional Associations. In the Adult divisions, these competitions are known as the USTA National Intersectional Team Events. In the 14 and 16 Divisions, these competitions are known as the USTA Intersectional Team Championships. In the 18 Divisions, these are known as the USTA National Team Championships.

title: Invitational Tournament
text: Invitational Tournament. A tournament in which entry is by invitation only.

title: ITF Rules of Tennis
text: ITF Rules of Tennis. The ITF Rules of Tennis are the rules for the sport of tennis. They are made by the International Tennis Federation (ITF). The USTA, as a member of the ITF, has agreed that the ITF Rules of Tennis apply to all USTA sanctioned tournaments.

title: ITF Tournaments on the National Junior Tournament Schedule
text: ITF Tournaments on the National Junior Tournament Schedule. The ITF Tournaments on the National Junior Tournament Schedule are tournaments jointly sanctioned by the ITF and USTA that are placed on the National Junior Tournament Schedule. These tournaments are played under ITF tournament regulations.

title: Junior Divisions
text: Junior Divisions. This group of divisions is comprised of the Boys’ and Girls’ 8-and-under, 10-and-under, 12-and-under, 14-and-under, 16-and-under, and 18-andunder divisions.

title: Late Entry
text: Late Entry. A late entry is one that is received after the entry deadline. Late entries will be accepted. In tournaments with limited draw sizes, late entries are accepted into a draw that is not yet full or placed on the alternate list after timely entries in the order received. Late entries received at the same time are ordered by a random drawing.

title: Layered Consolation
text: Layered Consolation. This is a consolation format in which the losers in each round are placed into their own consolation draw. Sometimes losers from two rounds are placed in the same consolation draw.

title: Let During a Serve (Service Let)
text:
Let During a Serve (Service Let). A service let occurs when:
• a served ball touches the net, strap, or band and is otherwise good;
• a served ball touches the net, strap, or band and then touches the receiver or the receiver's partner or anything they wear or carry before touching the ground; or
• the ball is served when the receiver is not ready.

title: The service does not count and the server serves again
text: The service does not count and the server serves again. A service let does not cancel a previous fault.

title: Line Umpire
text: Line Umpire. A Line Umpire is an official responsible for calling all shots directed to the lines assigned to the official.

title: Lucky Loser
text: Lucky Loser. A player who has lost in the final round of the qualifying tournament but who is allowed into the main draw when a player in the main draw withdraws. If there are many withdrawals from the main draw, a lucky loser may come from an earlier qualifying round.

title: Main Draw
text: Main Draw. The main draw is that part of a draw in which the remaining players have not yet lost a match.

title: Match Format
text: Match Format. The match format refers to the scoring format used by a tournament.

title: Match Tiebreak
text: Match Tiebreak. In some tournaments a Match Tiebreak may be played in lieu of the deciding final set.

title: Medical Timeout
text: Medical Timeout. A Medical Timeout consists of evaluation time as determined by the Referee plus a maximum of three minutes to treat a medical condition that is treatable. A player is not entitled to a Medical Timeout if the condition is not treatable.

title: Mixed Doubles
text: Mixed Doubles. Mixed doubles is a doubles match in which each team comprises a female player and a male player.

title: Mobility Device
text: Mobility Device. A mobility device is any mobility aid, such as a prosthetic, crutch or orthotics, used by a Para-Standing Tennis player.

title: Mobility Device Repair Timeout
text: Mobility Device Repair Timeout. A mobility device repair timeout is a cumulative timeout of up to 20 minutes that is permitted for mobility device repairs during a match.

title: Modified Feed-In Championship
text: Modified Feed-In Championship. This type of Feed-In Championship feeds the losers from the first two or more rounds of the main draw into a consolation draw.

title: National Adult and Family Tournament Schedule
text: National Adult and Family Tournament Schedule. This schedule is published yearly by the USTA Adult Competition Committee and the Adult Tennis Department and lists all National Ranking Tournaments other than Sectional Ranking Tournaments.

title: National Junior Tournament Schedule
text: National Junior Tournament Schedule. This schedule is published yearly by the USTA Junior Competition Committee and lists all National Junior Tournaments sanctioned by the USTA and ITF junior tournaments that take place in the United States.

title: National Ranking Tournaments
text: National Ranking Tournaments. These are the tournaments that are used for national rankings. Lists of these tournaments are found in the applicable USTA Tournament, Ranking, and Sanctioning Regulations.

title: National Standings List
text: National Standings List. This is a list of players used for selection and seeding to the extent permitted by the applicable USTA Tournament, Ranking, and Sanctioning Regulations.

title: National Wheelchair Tournament Schedule
text: National Wheelchair Tournament Schedule. This schedule is published yearly by the USTA Wheelchair Tennis Committee and the Adult Tennis Department and lists all National Ranking Tournaments other than Sectional/ Local Ranking Tournaments.

title: Net Generation PlayTracker
text: Net Generation PlayTracker. The Net Generation PlayTracker sets the requirement that players age 10 and under must progress through before they are eligible to play in a tournament that counts for Junior ranking.

title: Net Generation Programs
text: Net Generation Programs. Net Generation Programs are USTA-sanctioned events for players age 5 to 18 that do not count for ranking and are open to players regardless of residency, domicile, or citizenship.

title: Net Posts
text: Net Posts. Two net posts are used to suspend the net that divides the court.

title: Net Strap
text: Net Strap. The net strap is a strap that is placed over the net at the center of the net to make sure the net is at its proper height.

title: No-Ad Point
text: No-Ad Point. The point that is played at Deuce in a No-Ad Game to determine who wins the game.

title: No-Ad Scoring
text: No-Ad Scoring. This is a scoring system that is the same as the traditional system except that when the score reaches 40-40, only one additional point is played to determine the winner of that game. In Mixed Doubles, a male server serves this point to the male receiver, and the female player serves this point to the female receiver. In all other events, the receiver chooses the side from which the server must serve.

title: No Let Rule
text: No Let Rule. The no let rule, which is authorized by Appendix VI to the ITF Rules of Tennis, requires that a match be played without the service let in Rule 22a of the ITF Rules of Tennis.

title: NTRP
text: NTRP. NTRP stands for National Tennis Rating Program. The system rates players by ability levels ranging from 1.5 to 7.0.

title: NTRP Rating (computer rating)
text: NTRP Rating (computer rating). A rating generated by the USTA NTRP computer rating system based on three or more matches.

title: Numeric Scoring
text: Numeric Scoring. Numeric scoring consists of substituting “zero,” “one,” “two," and “three” for “Love,” “15,” “30,” and “40.” The principle of winning four points by a margin of two is preserved except when No-Ad Scoring is used. Deuce may be announced by “Deuce” or by “3-all,” “4-all," etc. Advantage may be announced by “Advantage" or “4-3,” “5-4,” etc. When language is a barrier, hand signals are often used with a clenched fist indicating “Deuce.”

title: Officials
text: Officials. Officials are Roving Umpires, Net Umpires, Line Umpires, Chair Umpires, Deputy Referees, Referees, and the Chief Umpire. Court Monitors are not officials. Tournament directors are considered officials only when serving as Referees under a regulation that specifically authorizes their dual roles or when serving as an umpire under the direction of the Referee.

title: On-site Alternate
text: On-site Alternate. An on-site alternate is a player not accepted in the draw who has checked in at the tournament and has asked to be placed in the draw if a spot becomes available.

title: Orange Ball Tennis
text: Orange Ball Tennis. Orange Ball Tennis is played on a 60-foot court with a stage 2 (orange) ball and a racket that is not longer than 25 inches. When adults play Orange Ball Tennis, they may use any length racket that is authorized by the ITF Rules of Tennis.

title: Ordered List of Alternates
text: Ordered List of Alternates. The ordered list of alternates shows the order in which the alternates are accepted into a tournament when there is a withdrawal. The Tournament Committee orders the timely entrants based on records or on time of receipt depending on the specific regulations that apply to the tournament or the information provided on the tournament website.

title: Para-Standing Tennis
text: Para-Standing Tennis. Para-Standing Tennis is for individuals with physical disabilities who can play standing without using a wheelchair.

title: Permanent Fixtures
text: Permanent Fixtures. Permanent fixtures include any scoring device that is attached to a net post, the areas of the net outside the singles sticks in a singles match, the doubles posts in a singles match that is using singles sticks, fences, backstops, curtains, seating areas, officials’ chairs, the ceiling, and lights for the court.

title: Personal Circumstance
text: Personal Circumstance. A bona fide reason other than illness or injury for not playing is a personal circumstance. Personal circumstance generally describes a situation in which a player has a serious or genuine reason for not playing. A Referee should give a player the benefit of the doubt when deciding whether the reason is bona fide. The inability of a junior to play because an adult who is not the junior’s parent or coach decides to go home is a personal circumstance. On the other hand, wanting to get home to play in another sporting event or for the convenience of the junior or an adult who is the player’s parent or coach is not a personal circumstance.

title: Place Playoff
text: Place Playoff. A place playoff is a match played to determine a player’s final place in the tournament, such as a third place playoff or a fifth place playoff in a Feed-In Championships. The winner of the FIC finishes in 5th place.

title: Playing Area
text: Playing Area. The playing area is the area inside the fences or backstops. Any designated seating or standing area is not part of the playing area. When there is a row of courts, the playing area includes the area between courts, but does not include any of the adjacent court or its doubles alley.

title: Point Penalty System
text: Point Penalty System. This is a system of penalties designed to deter unsportsmanlike behavior. The first penalty results in loss of a point; the second penalty results in loss of the game in progress; and the third penalty results in a default.

title: Points Per Round
text: Points Per Round. Points Per Round are the ranking points that are awarded in a Points Per Round Ranking System.

title: Points Per Round Ranking System
text: Points Per Round Ranking System. This is a method of ranking players or teams that is based on earning ranking points for the round reached, and in some cases, for wins over highly ranked players or teams.

title: Pro Set
text: Pro Set. A pro set is a scoring system consisting of one set only. The most common pro set is one in which the first player to eight games wins the match. If the score reaches 8-8, a 7-Point or 10-Point Tiebreak is played.

title: Qualified Medical Person or Trainer
text: Qualified Medical Person or Trainer. A qualified medical person or trainer is a person who the Referee authorizes to evaluate whether a medical condition is treatable and to treat players for treatable conditions during periods when treatment is authorized. Typically this person will be a physician, certified sports medicine trainer, or a person otherwise qualified by academic accomplishment, experience in sports medicine, or sports training.

title: Qualifiers
text: Qualifiers. Players included in the main draw as a result of their success in the qualifying tournament.

title: Qualifying Tournament or Qualifying Draw
text: Qualifying Tournament or Qualifying Draw. A qualifying tournament or qualifying draw is a tournament or draw in which those players who advance far enough earn places in the main draw.

title: Question of Fact
text: Question of Fact. “Questions of Fact” involve what happened. Examples include whether a ball is in; whether a ball touched a player; whether a ball bounced twice; and whether a server’s foot touched the baseline before the serve was struck.

title: Question of Law
text: Question of Law. “Questions of Law” involve the application of the rules or regulations to facts that have already been determined. Examples include whether an act was a hindrance, whether a player should have been assessed a code violation for misconduct, and the procedures for correcting e rrors in serving order, serving and receiving position, and ends.

title: Ranking
text: Ranking. Ranking is a static concept. It is a player’s “final” position at the end of a ranking period. It does not change at the end of the specified period.

title: Ratings
text: Ratings. Ratings are a system of categorizing or grouping players by their ability. Ratings are based on match results. NTRP is the official rating system for determining the levels of competition in USTA Leagues. JNTRP is a USTA junior rating system that helps match opponents of similar skill levels. Ratings are permitted for use in seeding and separating players into more than one draw. Any rating system may be used for seeding and separating players into more than one draw unless its use has been restricted by the USTA.

title: Reasonable Time
Recovery Rule
text: Recovery Rule. The Recovery Rule requires the Referee to offer a player two hours of rest after a singles match that uses a format consisting of the best of 3 tiebreak sets or more if the player's next match is singles. The regulation does not apply to short set matches, matches that play a tiebreak in lieu of a final third set, nor to any indoor match that lasts less than two hours.

title: Red, Orange, and Green Ball Tennis
text: Red, Orange, and Green Ball Tennis. Red, Orange, and Green Ball Tennis helps players of all ages learn tennis by utilizing specialized equipment, a smaller court, and modified scoring. Regulations for Red, Orange, and Green Ball Tennis can be found in the USTA Net Generation Tournament Regulations.

title: Red Ball Tennis
text: Red Ball Tennis. Red Ball Tennis is played is on a 36-foot court with a stage 3 (red) ball and a racket that is no longer than 23 inches. Red Ball Tennis is mandatory for tournaments in the 8 Divisions and recommended for other competitions in this Division. When adults play Red Ball Tennis, they may use any length racket that is authorized by the ITF Rules of Tennis.

title: Referee
text: Referee. The Referee is the official who is generally responsible for making the draw, conducting the tournament, and supervising all aspects of play. The Referee is responsible for assuring that the competition is fair and played under the ITF Rules of Tennis and the USTA regulations.

title: Rest Between Matches
text: Rest Between Matches. USTA Regulations require a Referee to offer a player a rest. The minimum amount of rest that is required to be offered is specified in USTA Regulation III.D. and Table 11.

title: Rest Period
text: Rest Period. Rest period refers to the time players may rest or are required to rest in best of three tiebreak set matches after players have split sets. The USTA Regulations require a rest period of 10 minutes after the second set in a best of three tiebreak set match in all divisions except the Adult divisions. In Junior divisions, the USTA Regulations also require a rest period of 3 minutes after the second set when a Match Tiebreak is played in lieu of the third set. The rest period requirements can be found in USTA Regulation III.D. and Table 12.

title: Retirement
text: Retirement. A retirement occurs when a player is unable to continue playing a match or resume playing a suspended match because of injury, illness, or personal circumstance. It is also treated as a retirement when a junior player does not finish a match because of adult discipline. A person who retires from a match remains eligible for other matches, including consolations, place playoffs, and doubles.

title: Round Robin
text: Round Robin. A round robin is a format in which a player plays every other player in the draw.

title: Roving Umpire
text: Roving Umpire. A Roving Umpire is an official other than the Referee or a Deputy Referee who exercises jurisdiction over one or more courts.

title: Scheduling Guidelines
text: Scheduling Guidelines. These are USTA Regulations that assist the Referee in determining how frequently matches should be scheduled and how many matches should be scheduled per day. The USTA requires Referees to follow these guidelines in most USTA National Tournaments.

title: Seed
text: Seed. This term refers to a player who is given a preferential position in the draw by virtue of the player’s record. The player is positioned in the draw so that the player usually will not play another seed until at least the third round. This player is more likely to receive a bye than players who are not seeded.

title: Seeding Groups
text: Seeding Groups. Seeding groups refer to 1, 2, 3-4, 5-8, 9-16, 17-32, and 33-64 seeds.

title: Service Courts
text: Service Courts. The service courts consist of the area between the net and the service lines. The service courts are bisected by the center service line thereby forming two service courts on each side of the net.

title: Service Lines
text: Service Lines. The service lines are the two mid-court lines that run from one singles sideline to the other singles sideline.

title: Set Break
text: Set Break. The set break is the 2-minute break after the end of each set.

title: Set Tiebreak
text: Set Tiebreak. The Set Tiebreak is the 7-Point Tiebreak Game that is played to decide a set when the set score reaches 6-all.

title: Short Sets
text: Short Sets. This is a scoring system in which the first player to win four games wins the set. If the score reaches 4-4, a 7-Point Tiebreak or a 5-Point Short Set Tiebreak is played. Alternatively, the sanctioning body may authorize a Set Tiebreak or Short Set Tiebreak be played at 3-all.

title: Short Set Tiebreak
text: Short Set Tiebreak. When Short Sets are played, a 5-point Short Set Tiebreak may be played with the first player or team to win 5 points winning the “Game” and “Set.” If the score reaches 4-all, a deciding point is played.

title: Sign-Up Consolation
text: Sign-Up Consolation. A Sign-Up Consolation is comprised of those firstmatch losers who chose to sign up to play in the consolation.

title: Single Elimination Format
text: Single Elimination Format. In this tournament format, once you lose you are out and do not get to play any additional matches.

title: Singles Sidelines
text: Singles Sidelines. The singles sidelines are the two lines that define the width of the court for singles.

title: Singles Sticks
text: Singles Sticks. Singles sticks are sticks that are 3 feet six inches high that substitute for singles posts in those courts that are equipped with doubles net posts. The centers of the sticks are located 3 feet outside the outer edge of the singles sidelines.

title: Solo Chair Umpire
text: Solo Chair Umpire. A Solo Chair Umpire is a Chair Umpire who handles a match without the assistance of line umpires.

title: Standard Game
text: Standard Game. The standard game refers to games in which the traditional scoring of “Love,” “15,” “30,” “40,” “Deuce,” “Advantage,” and “Game” is used. The standard game stands in contrast to the scoring for a tiebreak or No-Ad game.

title: Suspension Point System
text: Suspension Point System. This is a system under which players are assessed points for unsportsmanlike behavior in USTA sanctioned tournaments and ITF tournaments. A player who accumulates too many points is suspended.

title: Through
text: Through. A ball that is hit through the net is a through. If singles sticks are not used for a singles match, a through also includes balls hit through the open area between the net and the doubles post.

title: Tiebreak Game
text: Tiebreak Game. The tiebreak game is the term used by the ITF for the 7-Point Set Tiebreak that is played to decide a set when the game score reaches 6-all. In Red Ball Tennis, it also refers to one of the scoring formats that may be used.

title: Tiebreak Set
text: Tiebreak Set. This is the normal type of set that is played under USTA Regulations. A 7-Point Set Tiebreak is played when the score reaches 6-6.

title: Timed Match
text: Timed Match. A timed match is a scoring format whereby players continue playing until the end of a specified period of time has ended.

title: Toilet/Change of Attire Break
text: Toilet/Change of Attire Break. A player is allowed to take a Toilet/Change of Attire Break when an official determines that there is a genuine need. The player is allowed a reasonable period of time. When possible, the break is taken during a set break. If this is not possible, the break is taken at a changeover. Breaks taken at other times are limited to true emergencies.

title: Tournament
text: Tournament. Tournament refers to most forms of competition, including but not limited to, tournaments, championships, team championships, matches, exhibitions, events, intersectionals, international competitions, and zonals. It does not include regular USTA League Tennis Programs and USTA Junior Team Tennis but does include their championships. Most tournaments offer more than one event. Each event has its own eligibility criteria.

title: Tournament Appeals Committee
text: Tournament Appeals Committee. This committee is responsible for deciding appeals of the Referee’s disqualification or unilateral default of a player.

title: Tournament Area
text: Tournament Area. The tournament area refers to the entire tennis facility or center where tennis is played. It includes the area outside the fences surrounding the courts, any clubhouse or similar building, and the parking lot.

title: Tournament Committee
text: Tournament Committee. The Tournament Committee is the committee that is responsible for putting on the tournament on behalf of the organization that holds the tournament sanction. At a minimum, the committee includes the Tournament Director and Referee.

title: Tournament Director
text:
Tournament Director. The Tournament Director is the official representative of the Tournament Committee to the USTA, Sectional Associations, and District Associations; the chief executive officer for the Tournament Committee; and is directly responsible for all administrative details.
USTA Adult and Family Tournament, Ranking, and Sanctioning Regulations. USTA Adult and Family Tournament, Ranking, and Sanctioning Regulations are the regulations that govern Adult and Family tournaments that count for Adult or Family ranking.

title: USTA International Tournaments
text: USTA International Tournaments. USTA International Tournaments are USTA sanctioned tournaments played under ITF tournament regulations, but not sanctioned by the ITF.

title: USTA Junior Team Tennis
text: USTA Junior Team Tennis. This is a team competition for youth who are 18 years of age and under. USTA membership is required. Players advance from local to district, sectional, and national competition.

title: USTA Junior National Tournaments
text: USTA Junior National Tournaments. This is a group of national tournaments for junior players that are sanctioned by the USTA Junior Competition Committee, including the USTA Junior National Championships.

title: USTA Junior Tournament, Ranking, and Sanctioning Regulations
text: USTA Junior Tournament, Ranking, and Sanctioning Regulations. USTA Junior Tournament, Ranking, and Sanctioning Regulations are the regulations that govern Junior tournaments that count for Junior ranking. They are published on usta.com.

title: USTA League
text: USTA League. This is a program for men and women in which teams comprised of players with the same NTRP rating are established. USTA membership is required. Players must reach 18 years of age during the calendar year of the competition. Teams advance from local to district, sectional, and national competition.

title: USTA Level 1 Adult and Family National Championships
text: USTA Level 1 Adult and Family National Championships. These are the highest-level sanctioned tournaments in the Adult and Family Divisions.

title: USTA Level 1 Wheelchair National Championships
text: USTA Level 1 Wheelchair National Championships. These tournaments are the Wheelchair USTA National Championships.

title: USTA Net Generation Pathway Regulations
text: USTA Net Generation Pathway Regulations. USTA Net Generation Pathway Regulations are the regulations that govern USTA Net Generation Programs. USTA Wheelchair Tournament, Ranking, and Sanctioning Regulations. USTA Wheelchair Tournament, Ranking, and Sanctioning Regulations are the regulations that govern Adult and Family tournaments that count for Wheelchair ranking.

title: Voluntary Sign-Up Consolation
text: Voluntary Sign-Up Consolation. This is a consolation comprised of all losers from the first two rounds who choose to play in the draw.

title: Walkover
text: Walkover. A walkover occurs when there has been an administrative error or when a player decides not to play a match in an event because of injury, illness, or personal circumstance.

title: Waterfall
text: Waterfall. This is a method of distributing players into separate draws so that each draw is of similar overall strength. For example, assume there are four draws (A-D) and that the 16 players entered can be ordered based on standing, rating, or ranking. The distribution would be: A-1 B-2 C-3 D-4 A-8 B-7 C-6 D-5 A-9 B-10 C-11 D-12 A-16 B-15 C-14 D-13

title: Wheelchair Divisions
text: Wheelchair Divisions. This group of divisions is comprised of those d ivisions limited to wheelchair tennis players.

title: Wheelchair Repair Timeout
text: Wheelchair Repair Timeout. A wheelchair repair timeout is a cumulative timeout of up to 20 minutes that is permitted for wheelchair repairs during a match.

title: Withdrawal
text: Withdrawal. A withdrawal occurs when a player decides not to play all matches in the event because of injury, illness, or personal circumstance. A withdrawal also may occur because of tournament administrative error.

title: Yellow Ball Tennis
text: Yellow Ball Tennis. Tennis played with a yellow or white ball as defined in the ITF Rules of Tennis Section 3., and further referenced in Appendix I of the ITF Rules of Tennis.

title: Zonals
text: Zonals. These are team competitions held in the 12, 14, and 16 Divisions that are held in different regions or zones. Teams represent their Sectional Associations.
